text: The Embraer EMB 110 Bandeirante, meaning "pioneer," is a Brazilian twin-turboprop light transport aircraft designed by Embraer for both military and civil use. It was designed by French engineer Max Holste in accordance with specifications issued by the Brazilian Ministry of Aeronautics in 1965, aiming to create a general-purpose aircraft with low operational costs and high reliability for civilian and military operations. The aircraft was to have turboprop engines, a low-mounted wing, and sufficient capacity for eight personnel, based on a study of Brazilian commercial air traffic and existing airport infrastructure. This specification, known as IPD-6504, significantly influenced the aircraft's design. Early development predated the founding of Embraer, which was established in August 1969; construction of the prototype was supervised by Brazilian aeronautical engineer Ozires Silva, who also played a key role in founding the company. The first prototype, designated YC-95, made its maiden flight on 26 October 1968 from São José dos Campos Airport, piloted by José Mariotto Ferreira and accompanied by flight engineer Michel Cury, landing after approximately 50 minutes. Prior to this, 110,000 project hours were logged, producing 12,000 manufacturing drawings and 22,000 hours of structural and aerodynamic calculations, with an estimated 282,000 hours spent on manufacturing and tooling. The prototype was officially presented four days later, with a repeat of the maiden flight. The positive results led to the approval of production in mid-1969, with Embraer assuming responsibility on 2 January 1970. Two additional prototypes, designated EMB 100, flew on 19 October 1969 and 29 June 1970, respectively; however, due to shifting market conditions, the EMB 100 was quickly redesigned into the EMB 110 Bandeirante, which featured greater capacity and technological improvements. In May 1970, the Brazilian Air Force (FAB) placed an initial order for 80 production aircraft. The Bandeirante received its Brazilian airworthiness certificate in late 1972 and entered service with the Brazilian airline Transbrasil on 16 April 1973. A typical configuration seats between 15 and 21 passengers and is flown by two pilots; the EMB 110P1A/41 model has a length of 15.1 metres (50 ft), a height of 4.92 metres (16.1 ft), and a wingspan of 15.33 metres (50.3 ft). It has a maximum cruising speed of 411 km/h (222 kn), an economical cruising speed of 341 km/h (184 kn), achieving a range of 1,964 km (1,060 nmi) with 45 minutes of reserve fuel, and a service ceiling of 21,500 feet (6,600 m). During the 1970s, Embraer developed the EMB 120 Brasilia, an enlarged derivative with a pressurized cabin, greater speed, and capacity for up to 30 passengers, leading to the decision to halt further EMB 110 development and focus on the EMB 120. Between 1968 and 1990, Embraer produced a total of 494 aircraft in various configurations for diverse roles. The passenger model first flew on 9 August 1972 and entered commercial service on 16 April 1973 with Transbrasil. Ryanair operated a 15-seat EMB 110 starting on 8 July 1985, continuing until 1989. By October 2018, about 150 EMB 110s were still in service with airlines, air taxis, government entities, and air forces worldwide. Production ended in 1990, with the EMB 110 being superseded by the EMB 120 Brasilia. Deliveries to the Brazilian Air Force began in February 1973, with the first delivery on 9 February 1973. Two EMB 111A Patrulha maritime patrol aircraft were leased to the Argentine Navy during the Falklands War as a stop-gap between the retirement of the last Lockheed SP-2H Neptune and the introduction of modified Lockheed L-188 Electras. On 15 December 2010, the Brazilian Air Force flew its first upgraded EMB 110, designated C/P-95, equipped with modern avionics from Israeli firm Elbit Systems' Brazilian subsidiary, Aeroeletronica; at that time, the FAB had 96 active EMB 110s, which reduced to 48 by 2017. In 2020, 39 Bandeirantes were still in airline service with 15 operators: 31 in North/South America, 1 in Africa, and 7 in Asia Pacific & Middle East.
